transcript.text: The extractor fan over my hob has stopped working. Lights come on but the fan just hums when I press the speed buttons, doesn't spin. It's a Bosch chimney hood I think. Is that part of my hob?

No — the extractor/chimney hood is normally a separate appliance from the hob, even though it sits above it and may have been installed at the same time. It will have its own model/rating label, usually behind the grease filters or inside the chimney section.

Lights working but the fan only humming commonly suggests one of these:

• grease buildup or something stopping the fan/impeller turning
• a failed motor start/run capacitor
• a worn or seized fan motor
• less commonly, a control-switch/electronic fault

Turn the hood off at its isolator or fuse spur before checking anything. You can remove and clean the metal grease filters, then (with power isolated) see whether the fan wheel can turn freely. Don’t keep pressing the speed buttons while it only hums: a stalled motor can overheat.

For a Bosch hood, find the E-Nr/model number on its rating plate; Bosch appliance support or an extractor-hood repair engineer can then source the correct motor/capacitor if needed. If you rent, this would usually be something for the landlord/agent to arrange rather than a hob repair.

Thanks. I did notice a slightly warm smell when I left it humming for a minute or so. I'm not going up a ladder to take it apart, though, and I don't know the model number. Is there anything else I can safely check from the floor?

Yes: stop trying to run it. A humming motor that develops a warm/burning smell may be stalled and can overheat.

From the floor, the useful safe checks are limited:

• Turn the hood off and isolate its power — ideally at the nearby kitchen appliance isolator/fused spur (often a switch above the worktop or in a cupboard). If you cannot identify that safely, turn off the relevant circuit at the consumer unit. The hood’s own push-buttons may leave parts of it live.
• Do not keep testing it, even briefly, to see whether it starts.
• If the grease filters are reachable without climbing or stretching, you can check whether they are heavily blocked, but don’t put fingers or tools through them towards the fan.
• You can look from below with a torch for obvious loose material, but don’t attempt to turn the fan blades or dismantle anything while it is installed overhead.
• Check paperwork: kitchen installation documents, appliance manuals, landlord inventory, or a receipt may list the hood model. Otherwise an engineer can obtain the model from the internal rating plate.

Because the lights work, the supply is likely present; the hum points more towards the motor, its capacitor, or a jammed fan. The warm smell makes this a repair/maintenance call rather than a reset or hob issue.

If you notice smoke, crackling, a strong burning-plastic smell, or the smell persists after isolation, keep it switched off and contact an electrician/landlord promptly.
